concepts.plain: **p95** is the time 95% of runs finish within; **p50** is the median; the **tail** is the slow end. One huge run drags a mean, so artifacts 1, 2 and 5 publish none for skewed data.
concepts.analogy: Your usual commute is p50; the day the bridge closed is the tail. Their average is no real day.
concepts.why: A1 publishes no p99 (at about 100 runs that is one or two runs); A7 publishes p99.99 because every run has at least 200 messages above it.

concepts.plain: One curve of every run: time across, **share of runs finished by then** up. Every percentile, and the tail, reads off it.
concepts.analogy: Race results: at each clock time, the share of runners over the line.
concepts.why: A1's showed arm B's largest repeat-host run (148.2 s) beyond arm A's (111.6 s), despite B's lower median.

concepts.plain: **Spread** is where single runs land. A 95% **interval** says how far the **median** itself moves between re-runs: a plausible range for the true median. A **bootstrap** imagines the re-runs: it redraws the runs with replacement, 10,000 times, and keeps the middle 95% of medians.
concepts.why: A1's arm A interval spans a stretch where no run landed and excludes a value where nine did.

concepts.plain: Commit the hypotheses, analysis, exclusions and stopping rule **before the data exists**. The git timestamp is the evidence.
concepts.analogy: Sealing your prediction in an envelope before the match.
concepts.why: A1's predates its campaign data, not three paid reconnaissance captures, and says so; A6's campaign stays unread by its own rule.

concepts.plain: Run the arms close together in a shuffled order, so a slow hour or a drifting host hits every arm about equally. Arm A today, arm B tomorrow mixes the arm with the day.
concepts.analogy: Weighing two parcels on one scale in the same minute: if the scale drifts, the difference survives.
concepts.why: A1 ran 100 shuffled triples, one run per arm; A5 ran both traffic patterns inside every server start.

concepts.plain: A test, fixed in advance, that a model must pass against real runs before its answers count: **pass**, **fail**, or **inconclusive** (could not resolve its own margin; not a pass).
concepts.analogy: Checking a new scale against known weights, and remembering it was only checked up to the heaviest.
concepts.why: A2's and A4's simulators had to match three real repeats in at least half the time bins; A5's synthetic adapters, real ones within ±5%.

concepts.plain: A **forking path** is an analysis choice that depends on the data seen; unrecorded, no reader can discount it. An **amendment** is a dated, written rule change: what changed, why, what had been seen. One made after the data is still labelled post hoc.
concepts.why: A4's amendments are dated and say what had been seen: two came after its cell runs, before their analysis. A5's Amendment 3 extended its gate after an inconclusive verdict, and its post says so.

concepts.term: A failed gate is a result
concepts.plain: Publish the failure and every miss, with what is known of the cause. Measured inputs stand; the model's numbers may appear, but only labelled unvalidated.
concepts.why: A2's simulator failed twice, 34 of 37 judged bins missed, then 37 of 37; A4's missed 10 of 13, so its GPU counts are not validated.

results.title: Same two clusters, different split: the interval's width
results.axis: Width of the bootstrap interval on the median, in seconds. Two constructed clusters, 99 runs in all; only how many fall in each changes.
results.read_as: Near an even split, redrawn medians land in either cluster, so the interval spans the gap. At 70/29 they all land in the big one. Width follows where the median sits, not how far runs scatter.

results.title: Median versus tail, artifact 1's three cache set-ups

chart.note: Hollow circle: largest repeat-host run, given for A and B only.

results.axis: Seconds of total cold start, about 100 runs per set-up: p50, p90, p95.
results.read_as: The order holds out to p95, yet B's largest repeat-host run is longer than A's. A handful of runs, but the median ranking is not evidence about the far tail.

results.title: Three gate runs that failed
results.axis: Judged time bins per gate run; a pass allows at most half to miss.
results.read_as: All far past half. A2 missed on one side, then, calibrated, on the other; in A4's misses the simulator always predicted the engine slower than it was.

recall.q: What does a 95% bootstrap interval on a median range over?
recall.a: Medians of imagined re-runs of the experiment, not the runs themselves. It can cover a stretch where no run landed.

recall.q: Same two clusters: why does 51/48 give a 5.00 s interval and 70/29 give 0.00 s? Must intervals shrink with more runs?
recall.a: Near an even split a redrawn median can fall in either cluster, so the interval spans the gap; at 70/29 it almost never leaves the big one. Not necessarily: it shrinks only on average, and a new run can move the split toward even. A1's own data contradicted 'it shrinks as runs accumulate'.

recall.q: Why don't 10,000 more resamples make an interval more trustworthy?
recall.a: Resampling is free computation on the same runs; it adds no evidence. Only real runs, which cost GPU-hours, set the width.

recall.q: Why is a failed gate a result, and what may you still conclude?
recall.a: It is the pre-registered test answering no, which is its job. Measured inputs stand; model output appears only labelled unvalidated, and so does anything built on it.

recall.q: What separates an amendment from a forking path?
recall.a: The record: an amendment is dated in git and says what had been seen, so a reader can weigh it. Recording does not make a data-dependent change neutral, so one made after the data is labelled post hoc, like A1's first-touch rule.

recall.q: Why interleave arms instead of running each in a block?
recall.a: In blocks, drift over time lands on one arm and looks like its effect, inseparable afterwards. Interleaved, drift hits every arm about equally: it adds noise, not a bias.
